faults.finding: The chain from three currents to a climbing reading holds (R = V ÷ I, two of the three fade, so R climbs; leakage stays, so a wet core stays flat). But 'an absorption current flows while the insulation slowly polarises' names the cause without saying why polarising is a current at all.
faults.fix: Add one sentence: as the insulation polarises, charge inside it shifts slowly into line with the field, and that slow shift is the absorption current.

faults.finding: 'Cables have no such limit' asserts something no source here states. Screen 2 labels the arrows 'a few nanoamps', but the sketch's own dry core carries 78 nA of leakage and 199 nA of absorption at 30 s, so 'a few' is false.
faults.fix: Say IEEE 43 was written for machines, not cables, so it is a caution here, not a rule. Label the arrows 'nanoamps'.

faults.finding: Screen 3 draws the cause: the absorption current falling away above a flat leakage band, under the resistance curve it produces. Screen 4 shows both readings falling together, the cause of the steady ratio. Passes.

The check asks which of two cores with the same passing 1-minute reading has a steady leakage. It needs the why, not the name. The recall's third choice, '4.0, good', puts 4.0 in the wrong band on the notes' table (2 to 4 is okay), which muddles the slip it is meant to catch.
faults.fix: Make the third choice '4.0, okay' so only the subtraction is wrong.

faults.finding: Each figure he would look up carries one footnote: the PI and DAR bands, the makers' good thresholds, the halving rule, the 50-minute discharge, IEEE 43's caution and the low-capacitance PI. The contested points (bands, PI on very high readings, four or five times) are taught as contested. Passes.

DAR is used in the explanation without being named in words, and his notes call it the dynamic absorption ratio where makers say dielectric. PI and DAR appear in paragraph 1 before paragraph 3 introduces them. Screen 6 writes 0.5 × 0.528 µF × 5000², mixing a prefixed unit into the working.
faults.fix: Name the dielectric absorption ratio once, say it is also called the dynamic absorption ratio, and keep paragraph 1 free of the abbreviations. Write the working as the case file does: 0.5 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 5000².
